A tiny board costing around ₹250 can filter ads across your home Wi-Fi. No blocker installed on every screen.

Tech Heroes of India, Day 1.

The code comes from Egyptian developer ZedAxis, who shared the project on GitHub for anyone to use.

Someone built a free tool that keeps Claude working after you hit your limit. It’s called OmniRoute, and it sits between your coding tools and hundreds of AI providers through one endpoint. When one provider cuts you off, it sends your next request to another model automatically, starting with the free ones, and you keep coding without touching a setting.

Here’s how it works:

1. Install OmniRoute on your machine. It runs locally and gives you one endpoint at localhost:20128.
2. Add the providers you already have. Your Claude subscription, any API keys, and the free tiers you want in the pool.
3. Point Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or Cline at that endpoint. Same tools, same workflow, one new address.
4. Hit your Claude limit. OmniRoute notices and routes the next request down the ladder: your subscriptions first, then API keys, then cheap models, then free ones.
5. Keep working. It tracks what’s still available on every provider so you don’t have to.

What you get:

✅ 370+ providers and 1,400+ models behind one endpoint, over 150 of them with a free tier
✅ Automatic fallback the moment a provider cuts you off
✅ Built-in compression that trims the context your coding tool sends, about 89% fewer tokens on heavy sessions
✅ Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Cline, and Copilot
✅ Free, open source, MIT license, keys stored encrypted on your machine

Why this matters:
Hitting the limit mid-build used to mean stop, wait, or pay for the next tier. Now it means nothing happened.

caption:
Anthropic just built its own version control system because Git couldn’t keep up with its AI engineering workflow.

It’s called Scion — and the reason they built it is wild.
Anthropic’s engineers handle 30,000+ code changes a day, with a repository over 25 GB when compressed and around 25 million pulls daily.
So, seven engineers spent five months building a new system designed for that scale.
Here’s what makes it interesting:
→ 200× less infrastructure compared with their previous setup.
→ 100× faster pulls.
→ 25% more CI capacity freed up.
The idea is simple: the server stores everything, while clients pull only what they need.
And this points to a bigger shift in software development.
As AI agents write more code, writing code itself is becoming less of a bottleneck. Testing, reviewing, merging, and building infrastructure that can handle the volume are becoming just as important.
The future isn’t just about AI writing code faster. It’s about building the infrastructure that makes AI-driven development possible.

Here’s how to make your storytelling so addictive, it is scientifically impossible to skip.

This is called the Dopamine Addiction Loop.

It’s only 4 steps, but it uses the exact same psychology casinos use to keep you gambling.

Step 1 is the Stakes.

To have any dopamine release, the viewer has to care about the story in the first place.

To get them to care, you need stakes.

Stakes are:

1. A character someone can root for
2. Something at risk
3. Urgency

Step 2 is The Big Question.

This is where you give enough context to have a super juicy question pop in the viewer’s mind.

The stakes make them pay attention, but the big question makes them super curious and locked in.

In the casino, The Big Question when you’re playing Blackjack is which card is going to come next.

Step 3 is the Headfake.

And this is really where you hook them.

The headfake is where you contrast against what the normal viewer should believe.

So if my stakes and big question lead someone to assume A…I snap the story in a different direction to reveal B instead.

This is the art of contrast and what will make your story truly addictive.

Lastly, step 4 is the Rehook.

Just like a casino tries to redeal the next Blackjack hand as soon as possible, you want your stories to restart this loop again as quickly as you can.

Good stories have one addiction loop.

Great stories have many cascading throughout.

This combination of Stakes, The Big Question, The Headfake and The Rehook is all you need to tell a super addicting story.

It’s called the Triple Loop Method.

We all know most stories have a Hook, a Body, and a Payoff.

And there are tons of ways to write your script tactically…

Single Body format, Double Body format, Listicle, Tutorial

But the real secret sauce behind the best stories in the world is how they use open loops.

There are 3 main types of loops in all great stories.
1. Hook Loops
2. Intensifier Loops
3. Rehook Loops

Now the Hook Loop is designed to open the initial curiosity in the first 5 seconds.

And of course if this one doesn’t hit, the rest of the video is gonna flop.

But most people know about how to structure a good hook.

It’s the Intensifier Loop that most people ignore. 

Intensifier loops are designed to double down or intensify the intrigue from the hook.

Think of it like a curiosity magnet that literally pulls the interested viewer through the first 15 seconds.

Now the final one is called the Rehook Loop.

And this is really what separates good and great storytelling.

The Rehook Loop is meant to retrigger curiosity about halfway through the video, just as the initial intrigue from the first two loops is starting to fade.

The truth is, all great storytellers think more about loops than they do about structures.

And that really is the secret to telling addicting stories.

It runs locally on your CPU, so those internal screens never leave the machine. Worth knowing that coordinate-based automation is sensitive to redesigns, so expect to retest after a UI change.

caption: pov: you locked in for just one year

Changing one line on your website shouldn't mean opening a ticket and waiting a week.

That wait is the quiet cost of owning a website. Small edits pile up behind developer work, and every plugin you add to speed things up is one more thing that can touch your whole site. According to security firm Patchstack, 96% of WordPress security issues start in plugins, and WordPress powers over 40% of the web.

Cloudflare's answer is EmDash, an open source CMS, the dashboard where your pages and media live. It launched as a preview on April 1 and reached its stable 1.0 release on September 28. It's built from scratch in TypeScript, with no WordPress code.

Think of a building where every plugin gets a keycard for one room, not a master key.
Here's how it works:

 - Your team edits pages from an admin panel, no code needed
 - An AI agent like Claude, ChatGPT or Codex can connect through MCP, a standard way for AI to plug into software
 - When you connect Claude, you sign in and choose what it's allowed to do
 - Each plugin runs in its own sandbox and only gets the permissions an administrator approves
 - If someone has a page open in the editor, the AI connection respects that lock and won't overwrite their work

Cloudflare moved its own blog onto EmDash on August 12, part of its "Customer Zero" habit of using its own products first. Authors there can browse, create, edit, publish and schedule posts through EmDash's built-in MCP server.

Honest note: it's new. According to CMSWire, production use outside Cloudflare comes mainly from early adopters, people who try new tools first, and the plugin registry carries only free plugins for now. WordPress plugins don't carry over, though migration tools can move your content.

Here's my read: your website now has three kinds of users, your team, AI agents and plugins. The risk isn't any one of them. It's giving all three the same access.
Try this today: list everything that can change your website. Next to each, write the one thing it should never touch.
